title: What not to paste
objectives: Decide what is safe to paste into a chatbot, and remove the details that identify people or firms.

screens.prose: A junior analyst has a dull job: sort 200 clients by account size. A chatbot could do it in seconds. The list and names are invented.

lines: You: Here is our client list. Sort the clients by account size.
params.title: An invented example

screens.question: Before pressing send, what is the main risk?

options.text: The client data leaves the firm and may be stored or seen, depending on the provider
Only that the chatbot might sort the clients into the wrong order
options.why: A wrong sort is a risk, but a small one next to client data leaving the firm.

options.text: None, because the chatbot forgets each chat as soon as it ends
options.why: What is kept is set by the provider's policy, not by what the chatbot says or seems to do.

options.text: That it will be slower than sorting the list in a spreadsheet
options.why: Speed is not the issue. The client names, emails and balances are.

hints.text: What is in the pasted text?
Read the client lines.
Names, emails and balances of real clients would leave the firm the moment you press send.

feedback.correct: Client names, emails and balances would leave the firm. What happens to them next is up to the provider.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what the pasted text contains.

explain.text: Pasting sends the text to another company's servers. What happens to it then depends on that company's policy and your settings, not on you. A spreadsheet on the firm's own system sorts the list with no such risk.

screens.prose: Where does pasted text go? Slide through the steps. Which steps happen depends on the provider's policy and your settings.

state.caption: You press send: the text leaves your device for the provider's servers.

frames.caption: You press send: the text leaves your device for the provider's servers.
It may be kept there for a time, depending on the provider's policy.
Depending on the policy and your settings, it may be read by people or used to train later models.

screens.question: What decides whether pasted text is stored, read by people or used in training?

options.text: The provider's policy and your settings
What the chatbot says when you ask it
options.why: The chatbot's reply is likely text. The provider's policy decides what happens to your data.

options.text: How long the pasted text is
options.why: Length changes nothing about where the text goes.

options.text: Whether you delete the chat from your screen
options.why: Deleting it from your screen may not delete it from the servers; the policy says.

hints.text: Slide to the last step.
Read the caption.
The dashed boxes depend on the provider's policy and your settings.

feedback.correct: The provider's policy and your settings decide.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to the last step and read the caption.

explain.text: Once sent, the text is on the provider's servers. The provider's policy and your settings decide whether it is kept, read or used in training. Check both before you paste anything that matters.

canvas.caption: Depending on the policy and your settings, it may be read by people or used to train later models.

screens.prose: This is the **privacy risk**: what you paste leaves your device and may be kept or seen. So never paste passwords, personal data, client data or confidential figures, unless your employer's approved tool and policy allow it.

lines: You: Here is our client list. Sort the clients by account size.
params.title: An invented example

screens.question: Which of these is personal data?

options.text: A client's name and email address
The interest rate on a published savings account
options.why: A published rate is public and identifies no one.

options.text: A paragraph from a news article
options.why: A published article is public.

options.text: The formula for compound interest
options.why: A formula identifies no one.

hints.text: Which item is about one particular person?
Look at the second client line.
A name and an email point to one person: personal data.

feedback.correct: A name and an email identify a person: personal data.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for something that points to one particular person.

explain.text: Personal data is anything that identifies a living person, such as a name, an email or an account number. Public facts and formulas identify no one.

screens.prose: Sort ten things a colleague wants to paste into a public chatbot. All are invented.

rows: useful once names and numbers are gone
secret or confidential, whatever you remove

screens.question: Drag each item to its bin.

tokens.text: Text from a published annual report
Your own draft with no names
A complaint letter with the customer's name
A support ticket with a customer's email

hints.text: Which items are public already?
Which items are useful once a name or email is removed?
Public: fine. Names or emails inside useful text: remove first. Passwords, client lists and unpublished results: never.

feedback.correct: Public text is fine, a name in useful text comes out first, and secrets never go in.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask of each item: is it public, useful without the names, or secret?

byKey.password: A password is a secret in itself. Removing nothing makes it safe.
byKey.clients: The client list is the confidential data; with the names gone there is nothing left to sort.
byKey.results: Unpublished results are confidential until published, whatever you remove.
byKey.complaint: The letter is useful once the customer's name and details are gone.
byKey.notes: The notes can be pasted once the colleagues' names are removed.
byKey.ticket: The ticket is useful once the email address is removed.
byKey.article: A published article is public already.
byKey.maths: A maths question identifies no one.
byKey.annual: A published annual report is public.
byKey.draft: Your own draft with no names identifies no one.

explain.text: Public text and text that identifies no one carry little risk. Useful text with a name or an email in it is safe once those are removed. Passwords, client data and unpublished results are secret in themselves, so they never go in.

screens.prose: Before pasting a complaint to ask for a polite reply, remove what identifies the customer. The complaint is invented, and the bank's policy allows this tool for drafting replies.

lines: head teacher at the only primary school in Little Fennimore,
says her card was charged twice for £49.99
and that the branch staff were helpful.
params.title: An invented example

screens.question: Tap every line that identifies her.

hints.text: Which lines point to one person?
A job title plus a small place can be as good as a name.
Her name, her account number, and "head teacher of the only primary school" in a small village all identify her.

feedback.correct: The name, the account number, and the job in a small village all point to her.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which details, alone or together, point to one person.

byKey.l4: A double charge of £49.99 happens to many people; it does not identify her.
byKey.l5: Praise for the branch staff identifies no one.

explain.text: A name and an account number identify her directly. "Head teacher at the only primary school" in a small village names her just as surely. Replace them with "a customer" and the request still works.

screens.prose: A made-up chatbot has this setting. Read exactly what it says, no more.

lines: [x] Improve the model with my chats
When this box is ticked, your chats may be used to train future models.
Chats are kept for 30 days for safety review, whatever this setting.
params.title: An invented settings page

screens.question: Select all that apply: what does this setting tell you?

options.text: Unticking the box asks for your chats not to be used in training
Your chats may still be kept for 30 days
Unticking the box deletes your chats at once
options.why: It says nothing about deleting. Chats are kept for 30 days whatever the setting.

options.text: No person will ever read your chats
options.why: It says chats are kept for safety review. It does not promise who reads them.

options.text: Anything is safe to paste once the box is unticked
options.why: Your chats are still sent and kept for 30 days. Secrets stay out.

hints.text: Read each line on its own.
The third line applies whatever the box says.
The box is about training only. Keeping for 30 days happens either way, and nothing is promised about who reads them.

feedback.correct: It covers training, and says chats are kept for 30 days either way.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take only what the words promise.

explain.text: A setting promises what its words say and nothing more. This one covers training only; the 30 days of keeping happens either way. Read the real policy of any tool you use the same way.

screens.prose: A colleague asks a chatbot: "Do you remember what I pasted yesterday?" It replies: "No, I do not remember past chats." She says: "Good, so pasting client data is safe."

lines: You: Do you remember what I pasted yesterday?
Chatbot: No, I do not remember past chats.
params.title: An invented example

screens.question: Is she right?

options.text: No: what is stored is set by the provider's policy, not by the chatbot's reply
Yes: the chatbot itself said that it does not remember past chats
options.why: You took the chatbot's reply as a promise. Its reply is likely text; the provider's servers may still hold the chat.

options.text: Yes, as long as the data is from yesterday
options.why: Age does not matter. Whether the data was kept is set by the policy.

options.text: She should ask it a second time to be sure
options.why: A second reply is more likely text. Read the provider's policy.

hints.text: Who decides what happens to the pasted text?
The chatbot's reply is about the chat, not the servers.
A model not recalling a chat says nothing about what the provider stores.

feedback.correct: The reply is likely text. The provider's policy decides what is kept.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask who decides what is stored.

byKey.said-so: You took "I do not remember" as a promise about storage. The model may not see old chats, but the provider's servers may still hold them.

explain.text: A model may not see yesterday's chat, but that says nothing about what the provider's servers keep. Storage, review and training are set by the provider's policy and your settings. So the rule stands: client data stays out unless an approved tool allows it.

screens.prose: A team removes names from a staff survey before pasting it. Each row still has age, postcode area and job. Rows and places are invented.
screens.question: Tap the row that could still identify one person.

hints.text: Which row describes someone there may be only one of?
Think about how many harbour masters a small island has.
Age 62, a small island and harbour master together almost certainly point to one person.

feedback.correct: A 62-year-old harbour master on a small island is very likely one person.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which combination of details only one person fits.

byKey.r0: Many 31-year-old clerks live in a large city.
byKey.r1: Many 45-year-old analysts live in a large city.
byKey.r3: Many 28-year-old analysts live in a large city.

explain.text: No single detail in row 3 is a name. Together, an age, a small place and a rare job fit one person. Removing names is not enough when the details that are left combine.

screens.prose: Before pasting, both must hold: $$\text{allowed by the policy} \;+\; \text{nothing that identifies}$$ Passwords, client data and unpublished figures fail the first, whatever you remove. Names, numbers and details that combine fail the second, until you take them out.
screens.question: A colleague wants to paste a published fund factsheet to get a plain-English summary. Is that fine?

options.text: Yes: it is public and identifies no one
No: nothing from work may ever be pasted
options.why: Public, published text carries no privacy risk. The rule is about secret and identifying data.

options.text: Only after removing the fund's name
options.why: The fund's name is public. There is no person to protect.

options.text: Only if the chatbot promises not to keep it
options.why: A chatbot's promise is likely text. Here no promise is needed: the text is public.

feedback.correct: Public and identifying no one: fine to paste.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the two conditions.

screens.prose: A fund's rule: no client data or unpublished research goes into outside tools. An analyst wants a public chatbot to tidy an unpublished research note before it goes to clients.

lines: Fund policy, section 4: no client data or unpublished research in any outside tool.
Approved tool: the fund's own internal assistant.
params.title: An invented policy

screens.question: What should she do?

options.text: Use the fund's approved internal tool, or tidy the note herself
Paste it into the public chatbot after removing the fund's name
options.why: The research itself is confidential until published; removing a name does not change that.

options.text: Paste it into the public chatbot just this once, since the note is short
options.why: Length does not matter. Unpublished research may not go into outside tools at all.

options.text: Ask the public chatbot whether it is safe to paste the note
options.why: The chatbot cannot tell you what your fund allows. The policy does.

hints.text: Which tools does the policy allow?
Read the second line.
The fund has an approved internal tool. Use it, or do the job by hand.

feedback.correct: Use the approved tool, or do it by hand. Unpublished research stays inside.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read what the policy allows.

explain.text: Unpublished research is confidential, so it stays out of outside tools whatever is removed. Breaking a rule like this can break the law as well as the firm's rules. Check your employer's policy and the law where you work; here an approved tool exists, so use it.

ideas: What you paste leaves your device. The provider's policy and your settings decide whether it is kept, read or used in training.
Never paste passwords, personal data, client data or confidential figures, unless your employer's approved tool and policy allow it.
Removing names is not always enough: details such as age, place and job can combine to identify a person.

formula.name: Before you paste
formula.note: Both must hold. Check your employer's policy and the law where you work.

summary.trap: "It said it does not remember" is no promise. The provider's policy decides what is kept.

quiz.question: Which of these should never be pasted into a public chatbot?

options.text: Your work password
A published news article
options.why: A published article is public.

options.text: A general question about tax
options.why: A general question identifies no one.

options.text: A formula you are stuck on
options.why: A formula is not secret.

feedback.correct: A password is a secret in itself.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for something secret.

explain.text: A password is secret in itself: removing nothing makes it safe. Public text and general questions carry no such risk.

quiz.question: A chatbot says "I forget everything when this chat ends." What does that tell you about what the provider keeps?

options.text: Nothing: storage is set by the provider's policy
Nothing is kept on any server
options.why: Its reply is likely text. The provider's policy decides what is kept.

options.text: Chats are kept for a week
options.why: It said nothing about a week; and its words are not the policy anyway.

options.text: Client data is now safe to paste
options.why: Client data stays out unless an approved tool and the policy allow it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask who decides what is stored.

explain.text: The chatbot's reply is likely text about the chat, not a promise about servers. What is kept, read or used for training is set by the provider's policy and your settings.

quiz.question: A file has no names, but each row gives a date of birth, a full postcode and a job. Is it anonymous?

options.text: Not really: together those details can point to one person
Yes: there are no names anywhere in the file
options.why: Names are not the only way to identify someone. Details combine.

options.text: Yes, as long as the postcodes are real
options.why: Real postcodes make it easier to identify people, not harder.

options.text: It depends on how many rows there are
options.why: Even in a long file, a date of birth and a full postcode can single out one person.

feedback.correct: Details that combine can identify a person without a name.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how many people fit all three details.

explain.text: A full postcode covers one street or part of one, and a date of birth narrows that to very few people. With a job as well, a row can point to one person, so it is not anonymous.
